title: {{NAME}} and Princess Valor of the Iron Shield
moral: Strength is not just physical, it is the courage to do what is right when it is hard.

pages.content:
Princess Valor was the only royal in the kingdom with a secret identity.

By day: princess, as expected. Excellent at treaties, terrible at dancing, kept a sword behind her throne that everyone pretended not to see.

By night: the Iron Shield, protector of the merchant quarter, distinguishable by her armour and the fact that she always left before anyone could say thank you.

{{NAME}} was the only person who had figured this out, which was how he ended up as her unofficial logistics coordinator.

pages.content:
His job: know the city. Know where trouble was likely before it started, because the princess couldn't be everywhere and {{NAME}} could move through the city like water, unhurried and unnoticed.

He kept a notebook. He talked to market stall owners, night watchmen, delivery crews. He built a picture of the city that was as good as any map.

"You're a spy," Princess Valor told him once.

"I'm a listener," {{NAME}} corrected. "Very different."

She almost smiled.

pages.content:
The real test came when a gang tried to shut down the southern market by intimidating all the traders.

{{NAME}} had seen it coming for a week. He had also, quietly, arranged for every trader in the market to move their stalls two streets over on the same day, without explaining why, just suggesting it made business sense.

When the gang arrived, the market was empty.

And Princess Valor was waiting for them.

She had been there for an hour.

"Good information?" she asked afterward.

"Good listener," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
After the confrontation, as the night watch arrived to deal with the aftermath, Princess Valor sat on a market step and took off her helmet.

"I've been doing this for two years," she said. "Tonight was the first time the problem was solved before it became a fight."

"Preventing fights is better than winning them," said {{NAME}}.

"My father says heroes are measured by what they defeat," she said.

"I think they're measured by what they protect," said {{NAME}}.

She was quiet for a moment. "I like your version better."

pages.content:
He walked home thinking about the empty market square, the way the problem had not materialised because someone had listened carefully enough to see it coming.

In his room, he added the evening to his notebook and then closed it.

Protection was mostly invisible. That was the point.

He turned off the lamp and lay in the dark, satisfied.

Somewhere on the other side of the city, in a palace, a princess was setting aside her armour and thinking the same thought.
